meta.title: Redis vs Apache Cassandra: Which one to choose in 2026? (data models, performance & use cases & code compared)
meta.description: Compare Redis and Apache Cassandra architectural trade-offs, data modeling, query patterns, and indexing, and review side-by-side TypeScript to choose the right stack.

verdict: Choose Redis for low-latency caching, real-time analytics, session management, and scenarios requiring rich data structures and optional persistence. Choose Apache Cassandra for write-heavy, always-on applications needing linear scalability and multi-datacenter replication with tunable consistency. Redis excels in speed and versatility; Cassandra in distributed scale and fault tolerance. Evaluate your consistency, latency, and operational requirements before deciding.

comparison.toolA: Redis is an in-memory data structure store that supports strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes, bitmaps, hyperloglogs, and geospatial indexes. It also offers RedisJSON and RediSearch modules for document and search capabilities, but the core model is key-value with rich data types. This makes Redis highly flexible for caching, queues, and real-time features.
comparison.toolB: Apache Cassandra is a wide-column NoSQL database where data is organized into keyspaces, tables, and rows with partitioned columns. It uses a schema-based model similar to SQL but without joins or foreign keys, and it is designed for high write throughput across distributed nodes. The model is optimized for query-driven design, where tables are modeled around specific access patterns.

comparison.toolA: Redis stores data in memory and typically delivers sub-millisecond latency for read and write operations, making it ideal for real-time use cases. Performance depends on configuration, persistence settings, and network conditions, but it is generally faster for single-key operations than disk-based databases. However, dataset size is limited by available RAM.
comparison.toolB: Apache Cassandra is designed for high write throughput and can scale horizontally across many nodes, with latency depending on cluster size, consistency level, and replication factor. Reads can be fast when the data model aligns with query patterns, but complex queries may involve multiple partitions and increase latency. It is not optimized for sub-millisecond responses but excels at sustained throughput.

comparison.toolA: Redis offers horizontal scalability through Redis Cluster, which partitions data across multiple nodes and provides replication for high availability. Scaling is relatively straightforward but may require resharding and careful capacity planning. Redis Enterprise extends scalability with features like active-active geo-distribution, but open-source Redis has limitations in multi-datacenter setups.
comparison.toolB: Apache Cassandra is built for linear scalability and multi-datacenter distribution from the ground up. It uses a peer-to-peer architecture with no single point of failure, and nodes can be added without downtime. Data is automatically replicated across racks and datacenters, making it well-suited for globally distributed, always-on applications.

comparison.toolA: Redis provides optional persistence through RDB snapshots and AOF (append-only file) logging, allowing data to survive restarts. However, it is primarily an in-memory store, and durability depends on configuration; AOF with fsync can reduce data loss but may impact performance. Redis is not typically used as a primary durable database for critical data without careful setup.
comparison.toolB: Apache Cassandra is a durable, disk-based database that writes to a commit log and SSTables, ensuring data persistence even across node failures. It offers tunable durability with replication and consistency levels, and it is designed to handle disk failures gracefully. Data is not lost when nodes restart, making it suitable for system-of-record workloads.

comparison.toolA: Redis has a vast ecosystem with client libraries for most programming languages, managed offerings from major cloud providers, and modules like RediSearch, RedisJSON, and RedisTimeSeries. It integrates well with caching layers, message brokers (via Pub/Sub and Streams), and session stores. The community is large, and documentation is extensive.
comparison.toolB: Apache Cassandra also has broad language support and is integrated with big data tools like Apache Spark, Kafka, and Hadoop. Managed services are available from cloud providers, and the ecosystem includes tools for monitoring and management. However, the community is smaller than Redis's, and some integrations may require more custom development.

comparison.toolA: Redis is relatively simple to deploy and operate for single-node or small cluster setups, with straightforward configuration and monitoring. However, managing a large Redis Cluster with high availability and persistence requires expertise, especially in failover and resharding. Managed services can reduce operational burden.
comparison.toolB: Apache Cassandra has a steeper operational learning curve due to its distributed nature, tuning of compaction, repair, and consistency settings. Day-to-day operations require careful capacity planning, monitoring, and maintenance to ensure performance and availability. Managed services can offload some complexity but may limit control.

comparison.toolA: Redis is ideal for caching, session management, real-time leaderboards, rate limiting, message queues (with Streams), and geospatial indexing. It shines in scenarios requiring low latency and flexible data structures, such as gaming, ad tech, and IoT. It is less suited for large-scale durable storage or complex queries.
comparison.toolB: Apache Cassandra is well-suited for write-heavy applications like time-series data, messaging, recommendation engines, and sensor data ingestion. It excels in always-on, globally distributed systems where scalability and fault tolerance are critical. It is less appropriate for ad-hoc queries, joins, or small-scale deployments.

faq.q: Can Redis replace Apache Cassandra as a primary database?
faq.a: Redis can serve as a primary database for certain use cases when configured with persistence (AOF and RDB), but it is not a drop-in replacement for Cassandra's durability and distributed scale. Redis is optimized for speed and in-memory operations, while Cassandra is designed for disk-based, fault-tolerant storage across many nodes. For workloads requiring strong durability and multi-datacenter replication, Cassandra is generally more suitable.

faq.q: Which database is better for real-time analytics?
faq.a: Redis is often a better fit for real-time analytics due to its sub-millisecond latency and support for data structures like sorted sets and hyperloglogs. However, Cassandra can handle high-volume write streams and scale horizontally for batch or near-real-time analytics when paired with tools like Spark. The choice depends on whether you need immediate responses or can tolerate slightly higher latency for larger datasets.

faq.q: How do Redis and Cassandra handle consistency?
faq.a: Redis provides strong consistency in single-node setups and offers eventual consistency in Redis Cluster with asynchronous replication. Cassandra offers tunable consistency, allowing you to choose between strong and eventual consistency per query by setting consistency levels. This makes Cassandra more flexible for distributed scenarios where you need to balance consistency, availability, and latency.

faq.q: Is Apache Cassandra more scalable than Redis?
faq.a: Apache Cassandra is designed for linear scalability across many nodes and multiple datacenters, making it more scalable for large, distributed workloads. Redis can scale horizontally with Redis Cluster, but scaling is more complex and limitations exist in multi-datacenter deployments for open-source Redis. For massive write-heavy workloads, Cassandra typically scales more seamlessly.

faq.q: Which database is easier to operate?
faq.a: Redis is generally easier to set up and operate for small to medium deployments, with simpler configuration and fewer moving parts. Cassandra requires more operational expertise due to its distributed architecture, including compaction, repair, and tuning. Managed services for both can reduce operational burden, but Cassandra's complexity often demands more specialized knowledge.

faq.q: Can I use Redis and Cassandra together?
faq.a: Yes, many architectures use Redis as a caching layer in front of Cassandra to reduce read latency and offload traffic. Redis can cache frequently accessed data or query results, while Cassandra serves as the durable, scalable system of record. This combination leverages the strengths of both: Redis for speed and Cassandra for durability and scale.

faq.q: What are the licensing considerations for Redis and Cassandra?
faq.a: Redis is available under the Redis Source Available License (RSAL) for versions 7.4 and later, with earlier versions under BSD. Apache Cassandra is open source under the Apache License 2.0. For commercial use, you should review the specific license terms and consider managed offerings that may include support. Always verify licensing for the version you plan to use.

faq.q: Which database is more suitable for a startup with limited resources?
faq.a: Redis is often more suitable for startups due to its simplicity, low operational overhead, and versatility for common tasks like caching and session storage. Cassandra may be overkill for small-scale applications and requires more operational investment. However, if the startup anticipates rapid growth with write-heavy, distributed needs, Cassandra could be a better long-term choice.
